name: litellm

facts.description: The fastest, litest AI Gateway. Rust core with Python SDK. Call 100+ LLM APIs in OpenAI (or native) format with cost tracking, guardrails, load balancing, and logging [Bedrock, Azure, OpenAI, Anthropic, OpenAI, VertexAI, vLLM, Nvidia NIM]

title: LiteLLM: An AI Gateway for Routing and Governing LLM Traffic
answer: LiteLLM is an AI gateway from BerriAI that calls over 100 LLM APIs in OpenAI or native format, adding cost tracking, guardrails, load balancing and logging. It sits between your application and model providers, so it is infrastructure rather than a model or training library. The one thing to know before adopting it is that the project is mid-migration from a Python proxy to a Rust core, and its own incident reports document production outages and silent cost regressions tied to specific versions.

sections.body: LiteLLM is made by BerriAI and published at github.com/BerriAI/litellm under a custom licence, with its official documentation at docs.litellm.ai. It is a gateway and SDK rather than a model or a training framework. The site describes it as the fastest, litest AI Gateway, with a Rust core and a Python SDK, and the repository lists Python as its language. It sits in the serving and routing layer of the AI stack, between application code and providers such as Bedrock, Azure, OpenAI, Anthropic, VertexAI, vLLM and Nvidia NIM. The repository shows roughly 60,000 stars and a last push in October 2026, so it is actively maintained.
sections.heading: What it is and where it sits in AI work

sections.body: The gateway's concrete jobs are calling over 100 LLM APIs in OpenAI or native format, tracking cost, applying guardrails, load balancing across providers and logging traffic. The documentation shows reliability testing across providers with batch_completion_models_all_responses, which sends one conversation to every model in parallel and returns only the responses that succeeded, dropping models that raise rather than surfacing them as errors. It also documents load testing with load_test_model, which sends concurrent requests but always reports calls_made as 100 regardless of num_calls, and has no interval or duration options, so you loop over it yourself. Beyond routing, the site describes an Agent Gateway, a Model Gateway and an MCP Gateway under one control plane, with budgets at key, team, agent and customer levels. It is strongest where a team needs one endpoint in front of many providers with spend visibility and access control.
sections.heading: What it is used for and where it is strongest

sections.body: The Python SDK is the gentlest entry point, since the documented examples are ordinary Python calls against familiar model names. The gateway side assumes more: you need to understand HTTP proxying, API keys and provider authentication, Redis for caching and rate limiting, and deployment in containers or Kubernetes, because the incident reports describe proxy fleets, worker processes and OOM kills. No mathematics or model training background is required, since this is infrastructure rather than modelling. The official site offers tutorials, a blog, incident reports and reference documentation, but the material read here does not include a structured beginner course, so a newcomer should expect to learn from the docs and examples rather than a guided curriculum.
sections.heading: How hard it is to learn and what you need first

sections.body: The site documents integrations with Bedrock, Azure, OpenAI, Anthropic, VertexAI, vLLM and Nvidia NIM, and the gateway speaks the A2A JSON-RPC interface for agents, with OIDC and OAuth2 support for identity, including authorization_code flows with PKCE for per-user MCP credentials. It exposes headers such as X-LiteLLM-User-Id and X-LiteLLM-Team-Id so downstream agents can attribute spend correctly. Documentation is extensive, covering tutorials, gateway identity and FinOps, and a blog with tags for ai-gateway and incident-report. Community scale is suggested by the repository's roughly 60,000 stars, and the project publishes dev, release candidate and stable releases on a regular cadence, which the blog describes in detail.
sections.heading: Ecosystem and community

sections.body: LiteLLM serves both ends but is clearly aimed at production. The Python SDK makes quick experiments easy, and the batch and load testing helpers are built for evaluating providers before committing. In production the site reports that the Python proxy peaks around 359MB of memory under load, with CPU and memory climbing with concurrency and pods being OOM-killed at the worst time. The Rust gateway is presented as the answer, serving about 15x the throughput, 453 to 6,782 requests per second, on about 11x less memory, 359MB to 32MB, and cutting per-request overhead from about 7.5ms to about 0.05ms. The site commits to sub-1ms overhead and a sub-100MB binary. The cost of that control is operational complexity and a migration that is still in early beta.
sections.heading: Prototyping speed against production performance

sections.body: The site describes enterprise features including SSO and SAML, audit logs, spend tracking, multi-team management and guardrails, built for production, and its incident reports reference an enterprise customer running the database image behind nginx with a proxy fleet. That indicates real production use at scale, though the material read here does not name specific companies or give adoption numbers. LiteLLM is a current choice rather than a legacy one, given the active Rust migration and frequent releases. For someone choosing what to learn, gateway and LLMOps skills transfer across providers, but the project's own incident reports show that version discipline matters, since defects in v1.100.0 and v1.91.0 and v1.91.1 caused outages and cost regressions before fixes shipped.
sections.heading: Industry adoption and careers

sections.body: LiteLLM is written in Python with a Rust core, and the documented examples are Python, so it sits naturally beside Python application code and frameworks that call models. It is provider-agnostic by design, calling Mistral's API directly over HTTP via httpx rather than importing the mistralai SDK, and it fronts Bedrock, Azure, OpenAI, Anthropic, VertexAI, vLLM and Nvidia NIM. In a polyglot stack it typically acts as the shared gateway that any language can call over HTTP, while the SDK serves Python services directly. The site also positions it beside other gateways, benchmarking the Rust gateway against Portkey, Bifrost and its own Python proxy, so it belongs to the emerging category of AI gateway infrastructure rather than to model training or agent frameworks.
sections.heading: How it fits beside the others

sections.body: The documented weaknesses are operational. The Python proxy uses substantial memory under load and has been OOM-killed in production, and the Rust gateway that addresses this is in early beta, so its long-term stability is not yet established. The incident reports describe a Medium severity outage requiring an unreachable Redis plus failing providers, a silent cost regression that broke Anthropic prompt caching and raised spend 2-3x with no error signal, and a High severity set of incidents surfacing as full proxy outages in Kubernetes. The site's own benchmark of its classifier is explicitly caveated, with synthetic prompts, no independent review, and no claim of general accuracy. The material read here does not say how the custom licence restricts commercial use, nor when the Rust migration will be complete.
sections.heading: Limits and open questions
